transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-28 15:30 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Cardinal - Head Data Eng), Maya Chen (Cardinal - Security), Ravi Patel (Cardinal - PM)
---
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, um, quick intros then we'll get into the data handling questions for the POC, priya's gonna walk through how redwood handles logs and prompt storage, and then we can map that to your compliance needs.
[00:18] Daniel: great thanks Alex, yeah we're mainly trying to scope a 4 week POC, no production traffic, but it'll include real patient-support transcripts (de-identified-ish) and we need clarity on what gets logged/stored and how PII is handled.
[00:32] Priya: yeah totally, so high level for a hosted POC we default to transient request logs for routing/observability, but customers can opt-in/out of longer retention. Important bit is we have a few knobs: retention window, full request logging vs metadata-only, and prompt/eval storage. For PII you'll likely want request redaction + client-side pre-processing.
[00:52] Maya: can you clarify client-side pre-processing? legal wants assurance that raw PHI won't be stored on your systems.
[01:01] Priya: yup, so recommended approach is remove or mask PHI before send; we also support on-the-fly redaction rules in the ingestion proxy for common fields (ssn, dob, med record ids) — it's rule-based and can be tuned. Note: the automatic redactor is not a 100% guarantee, it's pattern/rule based, sometimes names or context slip through.
[01:23] Daniel: okay, we'd prefer redaction server-side because we can't change all our clients quickly. Is there a way to have Redwood run the redactor but not persist the raw prompts?
[01:33] Priya: yes, for POC we can enable redaction in the ingestion path and set retention to zero for raw prompt payloads. We can log an anonymized or hashed prompt id for tracing. That means no raw prompt stored after processing — but ephemeral in-memory copies may exist during inference.
[01:52] Ravi: what about the KV cache or prefix cache? If someone submits a multi-turn, does that persist?
[01:58] Priya: good question. KV cache is ephemeral and only lives on the serving node for the session; we don't write KV cache to durable storage for hosted POCs. If you opt for Dedicated or Private, different options exist (you can configure persistent traces but that's opt-in).
[02:12] Maya: encryption at rest and KMS? we need envelope encryption and customer-managed keys ideally.
[02:18] Alex: Redwood offers KMS integrations for Dedicated and Private; for hosted we do managed keys but we can provide customer-managed keys (CMK) in some enterprise plans — I'll attach the KMS doc. For the POC we can do a white-glove option: VPC tunneling + per-tenant encryption and limited retention.
[02:34] Daniel: latency is a concern: our success criteria includes 95th percentile < 400ms for short responses, can that be met if redaction happens server-side?
[02:44] Priya: yes, our redaction is lightweight; in our benchmarks it adds ~30-80ms depending on rule complexity. We'll include that in the benchmark run. If latency becomes an issue we can push redaction client-side or run a dedicated lightweight redactor in the VPC.
[03:00] Ravi: for the sizing: we're estimating about 30k tokens/day during the POC, but peak concurrency could be 6-8 qps. Is that enough to see realistic behavior?
[03:09] Priya: 30k tokens/day is fine for a functional POC. We'll recommend a benchmark run with synthetic load that simulates your average and peak — our standard config used in previous POCs is 50k tokens/day with 10 qps peaks to surface batching and latency.
[03:24] Daniel: okay please send the benchmark spreadsheet, we want to map token counts to cost and to whether caching will kick in.
[03:31] Alex: will do. Also note the caching behavior: prefix caching will reuse KV for repeated prompts; however prompt storage must be consented to for cache to persist beyond the session.
[03:42] Maya: on logging, our legal wants audit logs for who accessed what prompts and model outputs, but without storing the raw outputs long-term. Can you provide that?
[03:50] Priya: yes we provide audit trails: request id, user id, model id, time, and optionally hashes of prompt/output. We can avoid storing raw outputs and instead store a SHA256 hash for integrity checks. That meets many audit needs while avoiding content storage.
[04:04] Ravi: any limitations with streaming responses and function calls? we send structured data back to the product UI and want to ensure nothing leaks.
[04:12] Priya: streaming is supported; streaming frames are treated as transient data and are not persisted unless you turn on debug logging. For function/tool calling, the arguments/return payloads follow the same retention rules; be careful with debug mode which writes more detailed logs.
[04:26] Daniel: we have a long list of PII fields: name, address, dob, mrn, insurance id, free-text notes. We need to define redaction rules and test with real examples.
[04:36] Maya: and the retention policy — legal wants maximum retention 7 days for any request data and outputs must be purged after 72 hours unless flagged. Can your retention windows be that granular?
[04:46] Priya: yes, retention windows are configurable per-tenant and per-route; we can target 0, 1, 3, 7 days. For the POC we can set raw payload retention to 0 and metadata retention to 7 days. We'll also show how to configure purge jobs.
[04:59] Alex: let's talk about hosted vs dedicated POC. Maya, do you need the private deployment for compliance?
[05:06] Maya: for POC we're okay with hosted if we get the ingestion redaction + VPC tunnel + retention controls. If the POC proves successful we'll move to Dedicated or Private for production. We need evidence though — SOC2 docs and a technical walkthrough.
[05:19] Alex: got it, i'll send SOC2 + encryption docs. We'll also propose a canary plan: start hosted POC with hard redaction + retention 0, run benchmarks, then optionally spin a dedicated instance for a deeper security review.
[05:33] Priya: on benchmarking details: we'll run two main tests — 1) functional correctness with your sample prompts to verify redaction and outputs; 2) load test for latency/cost with synthetic tokens. We'll measure p95 latency, avg cost per token, and model quality regressions.
[05:49] Daniel: what's the time to get a hosted POC environment configured?
[05:53] Priya: we can provision a POC tenant in 2-3 business days after we get onboarding form and sample data. Benchmarks can run the following week. So timeline is plausible for a 4-week POC starting early May.
[06:06] Ravi: any shared artifacts you will send?
[06:09] Alex: yes: link - Redwood POC benchmark spreadsheet (will email), link - SOC2 + KMS integration doc, link - ingestion proxy redaction guide, and a sample config for retention.
[06:20] Maya: one more question — prompt storage and prompt-based analytics. We do want to collect aggregate metrics for model quality but not store prompts. Can you store embeddings or derived metrics instead?
[06:30] Priya: absolutely. We can store embeddings or hashed n-grams and quality metrics derived from prompts without storing raw text. That preserves analytics while protecting content.
[06:40] Daniel: good. Also we need the statement on accidental leak handling — incident response and notification windows.
[06:46] Alex: will include IR timeline in the security docs; typically 24-72 hour notification SLA depending on severity.
[06:53] Maya: ok thanks.
[06:55] Alex: recap of next steps: Priya sends benchmark config & runs after we receive sample; Alex sends SOC2/KMS docs and private deployment checklist; Daniel/Maya to provide data sample + retention legal notes. We'll reconvene after the benchmark results.
[07:12] Ravi: sounds good, thanks everyone.
---
Notes: transcription has occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "KV cash" for KV cache) and speaker overlap. References: security docs and benchmark sheet to be shared via email and CRM link.
